The central question is whether a continual fine-tuning system can maintain meaningful gradient signal across a heterogeneous replay buffer when task boundaries are latent or misdetected — specifically, whether the optimization landscape collapses into a narrow basin that satisfies replay loss superficially while catastrophically interfering with the current task's gradient direction. The key concepts are: (1) compositional coverage — whether the replay buffer samples span the full joint support of past task distributions rather than collapsing to high-density modes; (2) gradient interference — the alignment or anti-alignment of replay gradients with current-task gradients in parameter space, not just loss space; (3) task boundary detection failure — the condition where the system cannot correctly segment the incoming stream, causing it to either over-replay stale data or under-represent a genuinely new task distribution. The expert worry that beginners miss is the distinction between replay loss staying low and replay gradients being constructive: a buffer can achieve near-zero reconstruction loss on past tasks while the gradient vectors it contributes actively rotate the current update away from the loss basin the model needs to occupy — a form of silent interference that loss curves never surface. Compounding this, when task boundaries are misdetected, the buffer's compositional statistics become corrupted in a structured way — recent tasks get under-indexed, dominant prior tasks get over-indexed — and the resulting gradient field looks locally reasonable but pushes the model toward a weighted average of old tasks that generalizes to none of them. The hardest failure mode is when boundary misdetection is intermittent: the system occasionally identifies a correct boundary, giving the false impression that the coverage problem is self-correcting, when in fact the buffer's composition has already drifted into a configuration from which gradient interference is nearly irrecoverable without full replay reconstruction.

When the replay buffer has undergone compositional coverage collapse, the distillation target distribution becomes modally truncated — the teacher model's output distribution is only queried on high-density exemplars of past tasks, so the student learns to match soft labels on easy, high-confidence regions of the prior task's input space while receiving zero signal about the teacher's behavior on low-density but functionally critical regions like decision boundaries, rare constructions, or tail-distribution inputs. This is categorically worse than parameter-space forgetting in one specific way: parameter-space forgetting degrades performance uniformly across the prior task's input space, but distillation from a collapsed buffer degrades performance selectively on the exact inputs the buffer missed — the student appears to have retained prior-task knowledge when evaluated on common inputs but catastrophically fails on rare inputs, producing a forgetting profile that standard replay-loss monitoring cannot detect because the monitored samples are precisely the ones the distillation succeeded on. Hinton et al.'s original distillation work established that the information content of soft labels is concentrated in the off-peak probabilities at moderate temperature, which are most discriminative precisely at decision boundaries and low-density regions — exactly the inputs compositional collapse excludes. Empirically, Li and Hoiem's Learning without Forgetting demonstrated that distillation quality degrades substantially when the exemplar set is restricted to high-confidence samples, with downstream task accuracy on tail classes dropping 15-25% more than on head classes relative to full-distribution distillation.
